account: Vyntra's page metadata dates its “Fraud Cases” page to 4 April 2022, and the cases themselves are undated. The page states that “Our solutions stop the fraud before the money leaves the bank”. It lists about two dozen short case studies at unnamed banks. In one, an account takeover after pharming was stopped before a CHF 19,990 payment. In another, an impersonation led a bank employee to validate a CHF 1,000,000 transaction, which was blocked because the beneficiary was unusual at bank level. Other cases involve voice phishing, fake technical support, impersonation of a chief executive, business email compromise, romance scams and redirected invoices. The page says that payments of EUR 22,114, EUR 33,170, USD 7,500, GBP 21,000, EUR 125,000, EUR 170,000, USD 100,000, USD 170,000 and USD 850,000 were stopped in these cases. In each, variables of the transaction or the e-banking session (beneficiary, country, amount, currency, browser, screen resolution, language) did not match the customer's or the bank's usual profile. There are two internal-fraud cases. In one case “fraudsters were arrested while attempting to withdraw USD 500,000 (KSh 58 million) from the second bank's ATMs”. The models had flagged unusual timing and frequency of withdrawals. NetGuardians, a Swiss company, merged with Belgium's Intix to form Vyntra in June 2025 (FinTech Global, 19 June 2025). One entry on the page still names “NetGuardians solution”. The current page labels the CHF 19,990 example as Switzerland. No customer or bank on the page is identified, and the page supplies no dated event, regulator finding or court record. The page is the vendor's own account. In a separate, undated case study, Vyntra names Sidian Bank in Nairobi as a client from April 2019. In it, Sidian's head of internal audit, Peter Karichu, says that the software flagged rapid ATM withdrawals one weekend in mid-December 2019. He says that the fraudsters were arrested at another bank. Vyntra gives no amount for that case. The Sidian case may or may not be the KSh 58 million case.

fields.account: Vyntra's page metadata dates its “Fraud Cases” page to 4 April 2022, and the cases themselves are undated. The page states that “Our solutions stop the fraud before the money leaves the bank”. It lists about two dozen short case studies at unnamed banks. In one, an account takeover after pharming was stopped before a CHF 19,990 payment. In another, an impersonation led a bank employee to validate a CHF 1,000,000 transaction, which was blocked because the beneficiary was unusual at bank level. Other cases involve voice phishing, fake technical support, impersonation of a chief executive, business email compromise, romance scams and redirected invoices. The page says that payments of EUR 22,114, EUR 33,170, USD 7,500, GBP 21,000, EUR 125,000, EUR 170,000, USD 100,000, USD 170,000 and USD 850,000 were stopped in these cases. In each, variables of the transaction or the e-banking session (beneficiary, country, amount, currency, browser, screen resolution, language) did not match the customer's or the bank's usual profile. There are two internal-fraud cases. In one case “fraudsters were arrested while attempting to withdraw USD 500,000 (KSh 58 million) from the second bank's ATMs”. The models had flagged unusual timing and frequency of withdrawals. NetGuardians, a Swiss company, merged with Belgium's Intix to form Vyntra in June 2025 (FinTech Global, 19 June 2025). One entry on the page still names “NetGuardians solution”. The current page labels the CHF 19,990 example as Switzerland. No customer or bank on the page is identified, and the page supplies no dated event, regulator finding or court record. The page is the vendor's own account. In a separate, undated case study, Vyntra names Sidian Bank in Nairobi as a client from April 2019. In it, Sidian's head of internal audit, Peter Karichu, says that the software flagged rapid ATM withdrawals one weekend in mid-December 2019. He says that the fraudsters were arrested at another bank. Vyntra gives no amount for that case. The Sidian case may or may not be the KSh 58 million case.
